                        Abstract                                   Prominent finetuning methods, including supervised fine-
                                                                   tuning (SFT) [27, 38] and direct preference optimization
Preference-based finetuning of vision-language models              (DPO) [29], employ diverse loss geometries and super-
(VLMs) is notoriously unstable, i.e., trivially wrong nega-        vision signals, necessitating a unified analytical frame-
tives inject uninformative gradients that distort optimiza-        work to unravel their behavioral foundations, especially in
tion and degrade calibration. This work revisits this is-          preference-based alignment aimed at prioritizing human-
sue through the lens of learning dynamics and identi-              preferred outputs [31]. Preference-based finetuning is es-
fies a core pathology, i.e., the squeezing effect, where           sential for aligning VLMs with human intent [6, 20, 28,
easy negatives retain large, misaligned gradients despite          45, 52, 54, 56], yet it suffers from notorious instabil-
negligible loss. To address this, we propose Cooling-              ity in practice. Alignment datasets often contain static
Weighted Direct Preference Optimization (CW-DPO), a                or mis-specified negative examples (trivially incorrect or
two-stage framework that smooths and then stabilizes the           off-distribution) that inject uninformative gradients [5, 14,
alignment process. Stage 1 employs a constrained SFT               35, 46, 49]. These gradients disrupt optimization, de-
phase with low-weight “gentle negatives” to regularize             grade calibration, and produce overconfident, peaky pos-
overconfident distributions and flatten the loss landscape.        teriors. Off-policy methods exacerbate this by penalizing
Stage 2 introduces a competence-aware cooling weight               unlikely responses, while even naive on-policy approaches
that adaptively scales negative gradients according to the         struggle with gradient spikes from dominant “easy nega-
model’s average per-token log-probability, suppressing un-         tives” [7, 14, 50]. This points to a common flaw: align-
informative updates while emphasizing hard, on-policy con-         ment is often treated as a static optimization task, ignor-
trasts. This dynamics-aware weighting effectively mit-             ing the dynamic evolution of the model’s learning trajec-
igates the squeezing effect and enables smoother con-              tory [8, 14, 31].

mainstream benchmarks, i.e., COCO, Flickr30k, NoCaps,                 In this work, we adopt a learning-dynamics perspective,

Figure 1. Two-stage optimization process of CW-DPO. Stage 1 (y + Training) leverages positive supervision for stability but yields overly
uniform language styles (e.g., “A . . . on the . . . ”). Stage 2 (y − Training) introduces negative contrast for variation but risks errors (e.g.,
a running kitten as “flying”). CW-DPO’s cooling-weighted mechanism dynamically attenuates uninformative negatives while amplifying
hard ones, mitigating error propagation, and enhancing stylistic diversity.

                CW-DPO
Figure 2. our CW-DPO is designed to balance generalization and precision through a two-stage optimization strategy. In Stage 1, Smooth
SFT leverages positive samples together with negative samples containing minor errors to construct a smoothed supervision signal. This
broadens the model’s output probability distribution, thereby enhancing its generalization ability and robustness. In Stage 2, our CW-DPO
employs preference pairs with fine-grained errors for DPO. By sharpening the probability distribution, this stage strengthens the model’s
capacity for precise discrimination of critical details.

   Cooling Weight: Principled Modulator. To address                                     In essence, CW-DPO stabilizes training by smoothing ini-
this, we introduce the cooling weight wc , which adjusts the                            tial losses and refining preferences with competence-aware
negative-sample gradient based on real-time model confi-                                weights, as validated empirically in §5.

Top-5 generations. SFT-C sustains higher entropy (less squeezing) and overall quality.

                                                                         7. Conclusion
MMBench1.1, indicating the importance of smoothed ini-
tialization for stable alignment. Further removing negative-             In this paper, we uncovered core instability issues in VLM
sample constraints (w/o Negative Sampling) or replacing                  preference-based finetuning via a fine-grained learning-
the soft ReLU penalty with a hard constraint (w/o Soft                   dynamics perspective, focusing on the “squeezing effect”
Penalty) also leads to consistent drops, showing that both               that causes uninformative gradients and unstable optimiza-
negative-sample regularization and soft penalization are ef-             tion. Our CW-DPO provides a principled two-stage solu-
fective in alleviating overconfidence and improving gener-               tion, i.e., constrained SFT for loss landscape smoothing and
ation quality. In Stage 2, omitting preference optimization              competence-aware cooling weights to suppress easy nega-
(w/o CW-DPO) markedly reduces cross-task performance,                    tives asymmetrically and adaptively. Extensive empirical
confirming the need for competence-aware alignment. Us-                  results consistently and clearly demonstrate the strong su-
ing a fixed cooling weight (w/o Cooling Weight) achieves                 periority of our CW-DPO with faster convergence, stronger
near CW-DPO CIDEr but lower MMMU and MMBench1.1                          stability, and enhanced generalization.
